# Residential Night Support Notes

Fictional Cedar Lantern Dance Studio. Training fixture only; no real studio policy.

## Overnight cover
The night-support adult receives the current residential register and a private handover from the tour leader. The role begins at the recorded evening handover and ends when the morning lead accepts the group. The duty adult knows the escape route and carries the contact handset. A visiting parent helping with a daytime activity does not automatically become an overnight supervisor.

Residential night cover requires at least two awake duty adults until the final room check is complete. One adult remains near the desk while the other checks the corridor route. The requirement is about awake cover, not merely the number of adults sleeping somewhere in the building. If a duty adult becomes unwell, the tour lead arranges a replacement before either role is left uncovered.

## The evening timetable conflict
The night-support notes set residential-trip lights-out at 22:00. The tour leader handbook lists a different current time for the same trip and participants. These notes do not claim to supersede the handbook. Staff report both times and seek a decision from the trip lead; they must not invent a distinction between younger and older groups to make the conflict disappear. The final room-check procedure begins only after the confirmed timetable has been briefed.

## Rescue inhaler exception
A participant may keep a rescue inhaler on their person only when a written self-carry plan is signed by the guardian and medicines lead. The plan names the participant, inhaler and trip. It does not authorize self-carrying unrelated scheduled tablets. The tour leader's ordinary medication handover remains the default for items outside the recorded exception. Staff check that the participant knows how to request help without broadcasting the plan to roommates.

A participant using a self-carried rescue inhaler must check in with the night-support adult before the evening room check. This is a brief private confirmation that the item is accessible and the help route is understood. It is not a request to demonstrate a dose in front of the group. A buddy cannot complete the check-in on another student's behalf.

## Quiet time and late arrival
A participant arriving after the evening handover must be signed in jointly by the tour leader and night-support adult before joining a sleeping room. Staff confirm the actual arrival time and update the overnight roll. Do not mark a late arrival present merely because the family said they were on the way. A late arrival's bag can wait at the desk while the register is checked, without sending the participant alone along the sleeping corridor.

After the group settles, keep corridor conversations brief and away from bedroom doors. A participant who cannot sleep can use the supervised quiet seat by the desk. That seat is not a punishment and is not described as a breach in the class attendance register. The night adult records a factual handover note where follow-up is needed, and avoids writing speculative diagnoses or personal commentary.

## An unwell participant
The duty adult follows the agreed emergency route and contacts the relevant lead. The support notes do not diagnose an illness or set a universal medicine dose. A guardian's telephone advice is recorded, but medication follows the specific written arrangement and any appropriate emergency direction. Staff protect privacy while ensuring another duty adult can still account for the remaining group.

A moved sleeping place is recorded with the leader so that the morning roll uses the correct room list. Towels and a water jug can be provided through the desk, but no participant is sent into another sleeping room to fetch supplies. The support adult records when responsibility transfers back to the morning lead.

## Two contrasting examples
Rafi has a signed self-carry plan for a rescue inhaler and completes the private evening check-in. His ordinary scheduled medicine remains with the medicines lead. Bea arrives after the evening handover because her family collected her from a different event; both leaders sign her onto the roll before she joins her room. Neither case changes the document conflict about lights-out, and neither permits a staff member to infer a medicine dose. The purpose of these examples is to keep permissions specific to the named person and action rather than stretching one exception into a general waiver.

## Handset and desk notes
At handover, the night adult checks that the contact handset is charged and that the next lead's number is available. A personal phone can be a backup but is not the only record of the duty route. Desk notes record the time and action, with private medical detail kept in the appropriate folder. A note such as called the leader at the recorded time is more useful than a judgement about a participant's personality. If a paper page is corrected, preserve a legible record of the earlier entry rather than tearing out a whole shift.

## Morning transfer
The morning lead receives the actual overnight roll, any room moves and the location of keys. The night adult highlights an unresolved issue privately so that the participant does not have to repeat it in front of peers at breakfast. A sleepy student is given the agreed support route; the notes do not turn ordinary tiredness into a disciplinary offence. The morning lead accepts responsibility explicitly, after which the night adult can leave the duty position. A planned clock time alone does not prove that the handover occurred.
